claims.claim: The 1866 Atlantic cable's conductor was a seven-wire copper strand weighing 300 lb per nautical mile; over the roughly 1,700-2,000 nautical miles manufactured for the lay this totals on the order of two hundred (plus) tons of copper in the core.
claims.episode_span: roughly two hundred tons of copper in the 1866 cable's core
claims.source_title: Engineering Facts and Figures for 1866 - The Atlantic Telegraph (History of the Atlantic Cable & Submarine Telegraphy)
claims.supporting_quote: The present cable (1866, fig. 3) has for a conductor a copper strand of 7 wires, 6 laid around 1; weight, 300 lb. per nautical mile

claims.claim: The 1858 cable carried signals only briefly and was destroyed after about three weeks, when excessive voltage was applied to its degrading insulation.
claims.episode_span: The 1858 cable carried a detectable signal but degraded within weeks
claims.supporting_quote: The cable was destroyed after three weeks when Wildman Whitehouse applied excessive voltage to it while trying to achieve faster operation

claims.claim: The working cables cut transatlantic message time from about two weeks by ship to minutes -- commemorated in the slogan 'Two weeks to two minutes'.
claims.episode_span: The time for a message dropped from weeks to minutes, and the cost structure of moving information changed for good.
claims.supporting_quote: Line speed was very good, and the slogan "Two weeks to two minutes" was coined to emphasize the great improvement over ship-borne dispatches

claims.claim: The 1865/1866 cables were laid by the steamship SS Great Eastern, fitted out for cable laying.
claims.episode_span: the steamship Great Eastern was rebuilt with enormous cable tanks and linear braking engines
claims.supporting_quote: It was laid from the ship SS Great Eastern , built by John Scott Russell and Isambard Kingdom Brunel and skippered by Sir James Anderson

claims.claim: The 1865/1866 cable design used a central copper strand coated with Chatterton's compound and covered with four layers of gutta-percha insulation, wrapped in hemp and armor wires.
claims.episode_span: The cable was built with a central copper core surrounded by several layers of gutta-percha, then wrapped in hemp and iron armor wires
claims.supporting_quote: The core consisted of seven twisted strands of very pure copper weighing 300 pounds per nautical mile (73 kg/km), coated with Chatterton's compound , then covered with four layers of gutta-percha
